title: 閣僚更迭「高市1強」の弱点露呈
body: 政権発足後、初めての閣僚更迭は「高市1強」の弱点を露呈した。簗和生前農林水産相の無料バス疑惑や、参院での問責決議案可決の可能性など、更迭の判断に直結する情報が高市早苗首相には届いていなかった。重要な案件を一人で抱え込む首相の性質もあり、危機管理能力の不足は政権の行く末に影を落としそうだ。【主な経歴】簗　和生（やな　かずお）氏「首相に権限が集中し、周囲が何も言えない」。自民党幹部は政権の現状について、こう指摘した。首相は簗氏について、7～9日の衆参代表質問では「働いて仕事で返せ」などと続投を指示したと表明。だが、13日の衆院予算委員会で、簗氏陣営が衆院選で支持者を無料バスで運んだ公職選挙法違反疑惑が焦点になると、「きょうバスの話が出た。違法性があれば（進退判断を）ちゅうちょしない」と姿勢を180度転換させた。デイリー新潮や文春オンラインは9月末に簗氏の「予算カット」発言を報道。今月7日にバス疑惑を報じた。政府高官は13日の予算委後、「首相は週刊誌を読んでいないそうだ」と説明。「私は読んだが、いちいち報告していたらきりがない」と首相には伝えなかったと明かした。首相は公選法違反の可能性を把握しないまま、一度は続投を判断したことになる。また、自民関係者は「問責決議案が出れば可決されそうだということをつかみきれなかった」と証言する。与党は参院で過半数を割り込んでおり、野党が結束すれば可決に近づく。野党と太いパイプを持つ実力者の石井準一氏が、先の人事で参院幹事長を外れたのは首相の意向と見る向きが多い。政権の危機管理は首相の命運を左右しかねない。安倍政権では主に菅義偉官房長官が担当。萩生田光一官房副長官や今井尚哉首相秘書官と共に政府内と与野党に目を光らせ、機微な情報は安倍晋三首相に伝えていたとされる。失言した閣僚を数時間後には更迭したこともあった。高市首相は木原稔官房長官を重用しているが、安倍、菅両氏ほどの結び付きはない。自民内では、簗氏更迭で「首相の党内基盤が直ちに崩れることはない」（関係者）との見方が多い。ただ、閣僚経験者は順調だった政権の「逆回転が始まったかもしれない」と述べ、「このような事態が続けば来年秋の党総裁選はどうなるか」と漏らした。

title: 東京・福生で男性刺され死亡 逃走
body: 東京・福生市で18日未明、男性が刃物のようなもので刺され死亡する事件がありました。警察は殺人事件として現場から立ち去った男の行方を追っています。午前2時半ごろ、福生市福生で「1人血だらけの男がいたが立ち去った」「男性が刺された」などと通報が相次ぎました。消防などが現場に駆けつけたところ、男性（40代くらい）が左胸から血を流し倒れていて、病院に搬送されましたが死亡が確認されました。目撃情報などから男性は、50代くらいの男に刃物のようなもので刺されたとみられていて、その後、男は現場から立ち去ったということです。また、2人は知人同士とみられ、事件の直前には言い争う姿も目撃されていました。警視庁は殺人事件として逃げた男の行方を追っています。

title: 死亡事故 無車検の車運転疑い逮捕
body: 今月5日、愛知県愛西市で無車検の車を運転して事故を起こし、会社員の男性を死亡させたとして20代の男が逮捕されました。【動画で見る】「被害者を見捨てない」交通事故で重度の後遺障害残った患者を受け入れる専門病院 民間医療の“限界”を補完逮捕されたのは、愛西市の会社員・延末純容疑者(27)です。延末容疑者は今月5日午後7時すぎ、愛西市二子町松原の交差点で無車検の車を運転して軽自動車と出合い頭に衝突し、軽自動車を運転していた稲沢市の会社員・鈴木隆之介さん(26)を死亡させた疑いが持たれています。警察によりますと、延末容疑者も顔の骨を折る大けがをして一時入院していて、調べに対して「事故を起こしたことは間違いないが無車検だったことは知らなかった」などと容疑を一部否認しています。現場は信号のない交差点で、延末容疑者の車側に一時停止線があったということで、警察が詳しい状況を調べています。

title: 祭りで副市長が死亡 市長「痛恨」
body: 愛媛県西条市の難波江明広副市長(62)が17日夕方、地元の秋祭りで、重さが約2トンから3トンある「太鼓台」と呼ばれる山車(だし)の下敷きになり死亡しました。警察によりますと、難波江副市長は同日、西条市下島山の飯積神社の南側にある渦井川河川敷で大谷太鼓台の担ぎ手として祭りに参加していました。現場では当時、11台の太鼓台が共演する「かき比べ」が行われていました。午後5時45分頃、会場の警備にあたっていた警察官が祭り関係者に運びだされる難波江副市長を発見しました。意識不明の状態で新居浜市内の病院に搬送されましたが、約1時間後に死亡が確認されました。警察は、難波江副市長が太鼓台の下敷きになったとみて当時の状況を調べています。難波江副市長は7月に就任したばかりでした。訃報を受けて越智三義市長は「痛恨の極みであり、深い悲しみを禁じ得ません。故人のご冥福を心からお祈りいたします。市政運営につきましては、職員一丸となってこの困難を乗り越えて参ります」とコメントしています。

title: 息子が赤ランドセル希望 母の不安
body:
子どもの小学校入学に向けて、ランドセルを選ぶ「ラン活」。5歳の息子から「赤いランドセルがいい」と言われ、いじめにつながらないか悩む保護者の投稿が、SNSで話題になっています。そんな不安に対し、実際に息子の希望を尊重して赤いランドセルを購入した母親から、心強い言葉が寄せられました。どのような思いでランドセルを選び、子どもを見守ってきたのでしょうか。母親に話を聞きました。【写真】親は猛反対も「後悔はない」　6年間背負ったピンクのランドセル、実際の写真◇　◇　◇
発端となったのは、5歳の男の子を育てる保護者によるXの投稿でした。息子にランドセルの希望を数か月前から繰り返し尋ねると、答えは一貫して「赤」。本人の意思を尊重したいものの、男の子が赤いランドセルを持つことで、いじめのきっかけになるのではないかと心配し、購入に踏み切れないという切実な思いが明かされていました。この投稿に対して、SNS上では「子どもには好きな色を選ばせたいけど、心配になる気持ちはわかる」「いじめの不安がよぎってしまう」「今の時代、ランドセルの色でいじめられることはほとんどないのでは」など、さまざまな声が寄せられています。そんな中で「我が家ワインレッドのランドセルですー　特にいじめの種にはならずに3年生」と自身の経験を伝えたのが、30代の母親「ゆーみん」（@RRyuming）さんです。ゆーみんさんは、夫と現在小学3年生の息子、娘と4人で暮らしています。「ラン活を始めたのは遅くて、そろそろまずいなと感じた年長の夏から秋にかけて、近くのコクホーさんのショップへ見に行きました。ショップへ行く前から、サイトでランドセルを見た息子は『赤がいい』と宣言していました」実物を見てから決めることになり、そこで投稿者は、息子に付き添う役目を夫に託したそうです。自分が同行すると、息子が本当に好きな色や形を選べなくなるかもしれないと考えたためと話しています。「最終的に息子は落ち着いた赤のランドセルを選びました。特に問題はないだろうし、息子のセンスを信じようと思って購入を決めました。こだわりの強い子なので、そこで変に方向を変えても嫌だろうという思いもありました」それでも、心配がまったくなかったわけではありません。かつては、ランドセルというと「女の子は赤、男の子は黒」が当たり前で、投稿者自身もそのような時代に育ちました。息子が学校で浮いてしまわないか、少し不安を感じていたといいます。

title: 米の対露制裁見送り ウ大統領反発
body: ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領は17日、トランプ米大統領が対露制裁法の実施見送りを発表したことを受け、X（ツイッター）で、「米国の制裁措置の停止、侵略者への圧力緩和、金銭的支援、これらはすべてプーチン（露大統領）に攻撃を継続させるだけだ」と反発した。【図解】スターリンク、一体どんな仕組み？ゼレンスキー氏は、対露制裁法を巡り「残念ながら完全に無視するという決定が下された」と投稿。その上で「戦争を終わらせるためにロシアに対して真に効果的な圧力となるはずだった」と指摘した。これに先立ちゼレンスキー氏は16日、ブリュッセルで記者会見し、トランプ氏とプーチン氏が露産ディーゼル燃料（軽油）を世界市場に供給すると合意をしたことについて「受け入れられない」と改めて反対していた。会見で、トランプ氏との関係について「私たちは毎回話し合うべきこと、共に決断を下すべきことを見いだしてきた」としつつ、軽油を巡る対応については制裁解除対象が天然ガスや金融などへとなし崩し的に広がりかねないと批判した。会見の最後に、中間選挙が迫るトランプ氏から、燃料高やイラン情勢などを巡る自身の苦境から目をそらさせるための「スケープゴート（いけにえ）にされていると感じるか」と問われると、数秒間沈黙した。その後笑顔に転じ「これが答えだ」と言い残して会見場を去った。ゼレンスキー氏は、欧州連合（EU）加盟国の首脳会議に合わせてブリュッセルを訪れていた。会議では2027年の戦費は約1550億ユーロ（約27兆円）に上るとの見積もりを明らかにし、「現実的な額」として、不足する700億ユーロの追加支援を要請。コスタ欧州理事会常任議長（EU大統領）は、首脳会議後の記者会見で、追加の資金支援に応じる意向を示した。【ブリュッセル岡大介】

title: 米大統領 対露制裁関税適用を免除
body: 【ワシントン時事】トランプ米大統領は16日、対ロシア制裁法で、同国から原油や天然ガスを購入する主要国に課す100％の関税の適用を免除する大統領令に署名した。【ひと目でわかる】トランプ米大統領の支持率推移米国などへの軽油供給で合意したロシアに対し、融和姿勢を示した形だ。軽油価格の急騰は11月3日の中間選挙に痛手となっているだけに、危機感を強めている。法律は、ロシアの原油や天然ガスを購入する上位5カ国に100％の関税を課すもの。9月にトランプ氏が署名し、成立していた。免除期間は、追加措置を講じるのが「適切と判断するまで」として、明示しなかった。今月18日に導入される予定だった。大統領令によると、ロシア製品に対する500％の追加関税を含め、適用を見送る。「現時点でこうした免除を行うことが米国の国益にかなう」とする文書を議会に提出したという。法律は、対ロシア強硬派として知られ、7月に急逝した共和党重鎮のリンゼー・グラム氏が主導し、トランプ氏も成立に前向きな姿勢に転じていた。

title: 靖国に首相が真榊奉納 韓国は遺憾
body: 17日から始まった靖国神社の秋の例大祭に合わせ、高市首相が供え物の真榊を奉納したことなどに対し、韓国外務省は「深い失望と遺憾の意」を表明しました。【画像】高市首相、靖国神社の参拝見送りへ　真榊を奉納　秋の例大祭東京・九段の靖国神社では、17日から秋の例大祭が始まり、高市首相は「内閣総理大臣・高市早苗」の名前で供え物の真榊を奉納しました。19日までの秋の例大祭の期間中の参拝は見送る方向です。一方、17日午前11時半ごろには、城内成長戦略担当大臣が参拝に訪れました。これに対し、韓国外務省の報道官は、17日午後、談話を発表し、「日本の過去の侵略戦争を美化し、戦争犯罪者を合祀した靖国神社に日本の指導的立場の人たちが供え物を奉納し、参拝を繰り返したことに深い失望と遺憾の意を表明する」として批判しました。また、両国間の歴史問題について「真の反省を行動で示すことが、国家間、国民間の信頼に基づく未来志向の日韓関係を築くために重要な土台だ」と強調しました。

title: 中国車 ノルウェー軍情報を記録
body:
【AFP＝時事】ノルウェー軍の訓練中、中国製車両の車載カメラが軍事施設への入場コードや関係者の出入りなど、機密性の高い情報を記録していたことが分かり、コネクテッドカー（インターネットに接続し外部と情報をやりとりする車）がもたらすリスクへの懸念が高まっている。【写真】EUデジタル相、域外国への技術依存に警告「武器として利用される」 米中念頭
ノルウェーの経済紙ダーゲンス・ナーリングスリーブ（DN）によると、9月14～18日に首都オスロの空港で行われた警備訓練中、待機していた兵士らが車載ディスプレーを操作した際、車載カメラが撮影した動画を発見した。
動画には、車両を乗り降りする人物や走行経路のほか、軍事施設の門や扉を開けるための暗証番号まで記録されていた。
DNは訓練の3週間後に掲載した記事で、動画を撮影していたのはレンタカーだと報じた。少なくとも2台は、中国国有の自動車大手、長安汽車傘下の「ディーパル（深藍）」ブランドの車両だった。
これらの車両は、中国の自動車大手、吉利汽車グループが間接的に所有するレンタカー会社ハーツ・ノルウェーが軍に提供したものだった。
ノルウェー郷土防衛隊の報道官を務めるペールグンナー・グロスベルグハウゲン中佐はAFPに対し、「郷土防衛隊の兵士らが、車両のセンサーで撮影され、システム内に保存されていた動画を発見したのは事実だ」と認めた。
動画が中国をはじめとする第三者と共有されていたかどうかは不明だが、グロスベルグハウゲン中佐はその可能性を排除していない。
今回の事例は、欧州各国の軍がスパイ活動やハイブリッド攻撃への対策を強化する一方、使用する車両を通じて機密情報を収集される可能性があるという矛盾を浮き彫りにしている。
DNによると、軍は動画の発見後も、代替車がなかったため訓練終了まで問題の車両を使用し続けたとされる。
軍は中国製車両の全面的な禁止について、期待される安全保障上のメリットに比べてデメリットが大きすぎると判断した。

title: ロシア 最激戦地「制圧」と主張
body:
【モスクワ、キーウ共同】ロシアのプーチン大統領は16日、侵攻するウクライナの東部ドネツク州の最激戦地ドブロピリャを「制圧した」とゲラシモフ参謀総長から報告を受けたと明らかにした。軍司令部の一つを訪れ、軍幹部らに「ドネツク州の全域制圧に向けた道を開いた」と主張した。【写真】ロシアが核攻撃に踏み切ったらアメリカはどこに報復するか？　米政権内で行われていた机上演習の衝撃的な中身　22年
ドブロピリャはウクライナ軍がドネツク州の主要都市スラビャンスクやクラマトルスクへの補給路を維持する上で重要な要塞。制圧が事実ならロシア軍の攻勢に弾みがつく可能性がある。ウクライナ軍参謀本部は16日、ロシア軍がドブロピリャに「進軍を試みた」と発表したが、制圧は認めていない。

title: 通販に未認証のチャイルドシート
body: 国の安全基準を満たさず、安全性が極端に低いとみられる「チャイルドシート」がインターネットの通販サイトで販売されていることが国土交通省への取材で分かった。大半は中国製で、なかには「クッション」でありながら、チャイルドシート本体と誤認させるような紹介をする製品もあった。事故の際に命を守れない可能性が高く、国交省が注意を呼びかけている。【写真】アマゾンで販売されていた未認証とみられる「チャイルドシート」チャイルドシートは車の部品と同様に、道路運送車両法で保安基準が決められている。基準をクリアした製品には、国が安全性を認めた証しとして「Eマーク」が付く。道路交通法では、6歳未満の子どもについてチャイルドシートの使用を義務づけている。未認証品は、子どもを車に乗せる際に使うと道交法違反になる。国交省は2017年から通販サイトをチェックし、認証を受けていないとみられる製品があった場合、サイト運営者に対して商品ページを削除するよう求めている。同省によると、昨年度はアマゾンに25件の削除を要請しており、前年度から10件増えた。国交省によると、削除要請の対象となる商品のほとんどが中国製だった。出品者に問い合わせても、他社製品の認定証を加工した画像を出してきたり、問い合わせに応じなかったりするケースがあったという。一度は商品ページが消されても、同じような製品が別のページで売られることも多く、「いたちごっこ」の状態が続いている。国交省審査・リコール課の担当者は「未認証品の場合、お子さんの命を守れない可能性が高い。ネットで買う場合でもEマークがあるかどうかを確認してほしい」と話している。（増山祐史）

title: IMF高官評価 日本の消費減税法案
body: 【バンコク時事】国際通貨基金（IMF）のラフル・アナンド対日経済審査団長は17日までに時事通信のインタビューに応じ、日本の消費税減税法案を評価した。【ひと目でわかる】食料品の消費税率変更スケジュール物価高対策として来年4月から2年間の時限措置とし、給付金の対象を限定したことは「大いに歓迎すべき一歩だ」と強調。ただ、主要国で突出した水準の債務残高を抱える中、財政悪化にはくぎを刺した。食料品の消費税減税と所得に連動した給付制度を導入する法案は、9日に閣議決定され、衆院で20日に審議入りする。食料品の税率を現行の8％から1％に引き下げ、中低所得の勤労者を対象に給付金を支給する内容だ。アナンド氏は、「財源を賄うために追加の国債を発行しないことはとても心強い」と表明。「本当に支援が必要な人々に対象を十分絞り、恒久化しない措置」とする重要性を説いた。「非常に高い債務水準を踏まえて財政収支に（影響しない）中立的な形で実施すべきだ」と訴えた。長期金利の高騰については、債務返済費用の増加を懸念。社会保障費の拡大が今後も見込まれる中、「日本が十分な（財政）余地を確保し、債務残高の国内総生産（GDP）比率の低下傾向を維持することが重要だ」と提言した。日銀の利上げに関しては、「不確実性が高い中、非常に適切に金融政策を運営している」とし、今後も物価動向に応じて柔軟に対応すべきだと述べた。「円安が一段と進み、インフレ率が上昇すれば政策金利を引き上げる必要がある」と指摘。インフレ率は、今後数カ月間上昇した後、来年末までに2％の物価目標に向け低下すると見通した。

title: ソニー生命 50人を営業活動停止に
body: 複数の金銭詐取などが発覚し全顧客279万人への被害調査を進めているソニー生命保険で、金銭不祥事などの疑いのある社員が約50人に上ることがわかった。同社はこの約50人の営業活動を停止させた。被害調査はまだ途中段階で、不祥事の疑いのある社員数は今後変わる可能性がある。【写真】元金融庁長官のソニーFG社長が「おわび」同社では今年、複数の金銭不祥事を公表して以降、お金をだまし取られた、投資話を勧誘されたといった複数の申告が顧客から寄せられている。同社は4月から顧客の全件調査を始めた。5月には、営業社員だった4人が顧客14人から約1億2千万円を不正に受け取っていたと発表。その後も、保険業務に直結する金銭不祥事なども見つかり、社員数人の関与を発表している。関係者によると、これまでの発表分とは別に、約50人の社員に金銭不祥事に関わった疑いが浮上しているという。同社は調査の期間中、暫定的に営業活動をやめさせる措置を始めた。調査完了は11月末を見込んでおり、疑いのある社員数は今後変わる可能性がある。

title: 冷凍食品 高級化に異業種の参入
body: 10月18日は世界共通の管理温度「マイナス18℃以下」などに由来して、「冷凍食品の日」です。高級化に異業種の参入と進化を続けています。鮮やかな赤みが目を引くローストビーフに、濃厚なトマトソースのかかったロールキャベツ。実はすべて冷凍食品です。百貨店大手「松屋銀座」が今月から販売を始めたのが、コース料理の高級冷凍食品。銀座の老舗レストランの味を再現したメニューで、価格は税込み3万9960円です。松屋　冷凍事業責任者今井克俊さん「（銀座などの）名店の味を自宅で楽しんでもらえるような（商品）。高級グルメとしての冷凍食品（市場）は少しずつ伸びている」4年前に始まったこの事業は、今では年間1億円の売り上げにまで拡大。自宅用やギフト用で人気が高まっているといいます。買い物客「冷凍技術がそこまで進化しているんですね。食べてみたいです」こうしたなか、意外な巨大企業が勝負に出ました。高級冷凍食品に目をつけたのが、大手デベロッパーの三井不動産でした。mitaseru JAPAN　松本大輝代表「ここが日本橋の老舗料理店の味を再現して高級冷凍食品を製造している場所」三井不動産は、2年前に高級冷凍食品事業を手掛ける子会社を立ち上げました。運営する商業施設に入る店の味を再現した冷凍食品をオンラインなどで販売しています。コロナ禍で飲食店が苦境に立つなか、新たな収益源として冷凍食品に行き着いたといいます。松本代表「（三井不動産は）商業施設を多く運営していて、そこにいろいろな名店が出店している。そのような当社の強みを生かして（事業をしている）」飲食店との関係から物流まで、ディベロッパーならではの強みを生かした戦略で、来月には千葉県に2カ所目の拠点を稼働させます。さらに会社は海外展開を視野に、シンガポールでテスト販売を開始しました。松本代表「訪日客が多くなってきているので、日本に来なくても名店の味を届けられるように（したい）」将来的には台湾などへも販路を拡大し育てていく狙いだということです。

title: 住宅ローン金利上昇 今できること
body:
「住宅ローンの金利が上がったら、わが家の返済額はどうなる？」住宅ローンを返済中の人なら、一度は気になったことがあるのではないでしょうか。金利の上昇がニュースになるたびに、「このまま変動金利で大丈夫？」「固定金利に変えたほうがいい？」「借り換えを検討するべき？」と、不安を感じる人も少なくありません。【画像一覧】小さな金利上昇から大きな影響が！？将来の安心につながる家計の見直し方とは住宅ローンは、多くの家庭にとって人生で最も大きな借り入れです。そのため、返済額が増えると不安になるのは当然のことです。一方で、「固定金利にすべき」「すぐに借り換えをしましょう」といった意見を目にすることもあります。家庭の事情は、家庭の数だけ異なります。大切なのは情報に振り回されることではなく、わが家にとって最適な選択は何かを考えることです。この記事では、住宅ローン金利が上がる時代に家計を守るための考え方について、ファイナンシャルプランナーが解説します。「隣の女性」のリアルな本音を伝え、「今」を生きる女性たちを応援したい――。そんな思いからCBCテレビが立ち上げたのが、「me:tone編集部」です。
まず知っておきたいのは、金利の上昇は住宅ローンを利用しているすべての人に同じ影響があるわけではないということです。固定金利で借りている方は、契約時に決まった金利が返済終了まで続くため、基本的には金利が上がっても毎月の返済額は変わりません。そして、変動金利は市場金利の動向に応じて見直されるため、将来的に返済額が増える可能性があります。金利が増えるからといって、変動金利が危険というわけではありません。変動金利は、固定金利よりも低い金利で推移してきたため、多くの方が恩恵を受けてきました。大切なのは、自分の住宅ローンの内容を理解し、家計への影響を把握しておくことです。
「金利が0.25％上昇する」と聞いてもピンと来ない人も多いかと思います。「0.25％しか上がらないなら、それほど変わらないのでは」と思う方もいるかもしれません。しかし、住宅ローンは借入額が大きく、返済期間も長いため、小さな金利差でも総返済額には大きな違いが生まれます。例えば、借入残高3,000万円、返済期間20年程度の場合、金利が0.25％上昇すると、月々3,000円程度の返済額が増えるケースがあります。月々3,000円程度増えるだけなら大きな負担ではないように感じるかもしれませんが、年間で約36,000円、10年続けば、約36万円になります。さらに、食料品や日用品、電気・ガス代など、暮らしに欠かせないものの値上がりも続いています。月々の住宅ローン返済額だけを見れば小さな変化でも、さまざまな支出が重なることで家計への負担は少しずつ大きくなっていくのです。

title: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze in France as over 1,000 arrested after protests
summary: Disorder broke out in cities across the country on a day in which more than half a million joined cost of living protests.
body:
How day of protests unfolded as disorder breaks out across France
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.
In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.
Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.
Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.
La Barrique bar in Paris was set on fire
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.
In Paris, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC they were "pacifists" who are "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".
However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.
Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
A car was set alight at the Place de la République in Paris
In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy" for the city, telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.
Limoges town hall was "largely lost" in a blaze, the prefecture said
A young man "had his hand blown off by a grenade" in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."
The interior ministry said the protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.
Rapid-response riot police were deployed in Paris
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
On Saturday, their numbers were bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.
These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes 'yellow vest' movement, who demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.
French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.
The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.
Shops were looted in Paris, and other cities, during demonstrations on Saturday
Watch: 'The mood has really shifted' at the Paris student protests
Prime Minister Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".
He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."
Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.
Police fired water cannon at protesters in the Place de la République, Paris
French President Emmanuel Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers, during a television interview on 8 October.
However, the protests have continued and intensified.

title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
summary: The US president temporarily ends many restrictions on Moscow recently passed by Congress over "national security" concerns.
body:
Donald Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky deepens.
The sanctions were passed by the Congress and signed into law the president in September.
But Trump issued an executive order Friday night saying that suspending some was in the US national interest, prompting a backlash from US lawmakers. Zelensky said it was unfortunate the US has decided to "completely disregard" the sanctions.
Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed afterthe US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesellast week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Trump and Zelensky have exchanged sharp words about one another. Ukraine's president declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing an EU summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The new US sanctions law took aim at Russia's economy by giving Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
It also included sanctions against senior Russian figures, including Putin, as well as Russian financial institutions and Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of vessels used to circumvent existing embargoes.
Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
Many of these provisions have now been waived by Trump.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the waiver "an important and truly historic moment".
Posting on X, he said the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage", primarily on the US and global market, and that economic cooperation benefits both nations.
Democrats including the Virginia Congressman Don Beyer criticised the move, accusing Trump of capitulating to Moscow and turning his back on Kyiv and Zelensky.
"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer wrote on X.
A handful of Republicans, too, have come out against the move.
Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, a Trump ally, called waving sanctions against Russia a mistake, saying on Fox News: "I wish the president hadn't done it."
He added there were other ways to could address diesel prices and "the current path, unfortunately, just... benefits Putin and that's not a good idea."
Senator John Cornyn, also of Texas, said on X: "Helping Putin in Ukraine is reckless. He would not stop with Ukraine and our NATO allies would be next."
North Carolina Senator Thom Tillis called it "beyond irresponsible", noting the sanctions legislation passed the chamber with bipartisan support and a large majority - only 11 senators voted against it.
Trump could bring down energy prices "by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin," he said.
Nebraska Representative Don Bacon said many lawmakers will resist funding the president's agenda "knowing he is propping up a dictator's invasion and throwing an ally under the bus".
The move is likely to draw further anger from Ukraine, where Zelensky has long stressed the need for stringent sanctions to limit funding Russia can use in its war effort.
Zelensky said on Saturday morning that the sanctions "could have helped enormously" and that the law was "supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end".
He pointed to Russian overnight attacks on 15 Ukrainian energy facilities that had caused power cuts in several regions and said: "Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine – right before winter."
Zelensky said it was "important that everyone in America also sees what is really happening" on the ground.
Watch: Will Ukraine get the support needed as tensions with US rise?
He later told reporters that he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.
Negotiators from Ukraine spoke to their US counterparts on Friday and that both teams could meet next week, he also said.
Trump was initially criticised by Zelensky and Ukraine's European allies for temporarily suspending some US sanctions to import Russian diesel in a bid to bring down US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war. His Republican party is at risk of losing control of the US Congress, in next month's midterm elections, largely due to voters' sour mood about affordability.
Zelensky suggested the deal was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.
A few days later, Trump claimed that both Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to facilitate the export of Russian diesel.
Both nations have been intensively striking one another's energy infrastructure. Kyiv says this is to limit revenue for Russia's war machine, while Moscow claims it only targets facilities used by the Ukrainian military.
Zelensky initially expressed surprise at Trump's announcement, and said Kyiv would stop the strikes if Russia did the same. After three days of fresh attacks from Russia, Kyiv resumed its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump, condemned Ukraine's strikes as a disgrace, but Zelensky said he was "only standing up for Ukraine's interests".
Zaporizhzhia was among regions hit by Russian strikes overnight
Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine.
Last weekStarlink suddenly and unexpectedly restrictedthe speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection. This disrupted some battlefield missions, Ukraine said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
During the slowdown, Russia launched several deadly strikes on Ukraine, with residents and the government saying these came with no prior warning.
Zelensky told reporters on Saturday that Ukraine had been told by US officials the speed restrictions were linked to technical issues.
However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found "these problems do not exist" and the system was operating at higher speeds.
Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharingand deliberately slowing down the network.
Ukrainian authorities have confirmed that at least nine people have been killed and around 60 injured in Russian strikes across the country over the past 24 hours. That included an ambulance driver killed and 20 others injured in a Russian strike on the city of Kherson, they said.
Russia's defence ministry said it had targeted industries linked to Ukraine's defence industry - including steel works, an electrical sub-station and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea.

title: European diplomats attacked by Israeli settlers in West Bank
summary: The Israeli military condemns the violence but the prime minister's office says it is part of a "smear" campaign.
body:
Masked settlers are accused of attacking the convoy
A delegation of European diplomats has been attacked by masked Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Belgium condemned the assault on its consul general and the other envoys and called for Israel to bring those responsible to justice.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) also condemned what they called "the severe act of violence" and said they were investigating.
But the office of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu cast doubt on what happened and suggested it was part of a "coordinated campaign to smear Israel".
The attack came only a day after a number of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photographer, were injured in a separate assault by settlers in another village in the West Bank.
The diplomats - from Belgium, France, Poland and the Catholic Church - had come to the largely Christian village of Taybeh near Ramallah.
They were there to assess the situation on the ground after almost near daily attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest.
Video footage from the scene showed masked settlers confronting the convoy. Reports suggest stones were thrown.
The Belgian authorities said a car from its consulate had a window smashed and a French mayor was assaulted. Video showed a man wearing a French tricolor sash slumped beside a vehicle.
Belgium's foreign minister Maxime Prevot condemned the attack and said Israel had a responsibility to bring those responsible to justice.
"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," he said.
"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice.
"Impunity for violent settlers must end. Belgium will continue to press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them."
Gideon Sa'ar, Israel's foreign minister, said he strongly condemned the violence by what he called "Israeli rioters". He said the foreign ministry was in contact with the ambassadors of the countries involved.
But he added: "Without detracting from the severity of the incident, it is unfortunate that the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors' security."
The IDF said they "strongly condemn the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters."
"According to a preliminary inquiry, no IDF soldiers were present at the scene at the time of the attack," they added.
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux, the left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries
But Netanyahu's office urged "caution before drawing conclusions" from reports about the attack.
It said the images on social media "do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility".
A statement continued: "Those circumstances remain under investigation. Israeli police and forensic investigators have launched an investigation to establish the facts and identify those responsible."
It added that "these reports come amid concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria during the annual olive harvest, relying on sensational headlines before the full facts emerge".
Netanyahu's office named the injured French official as Bernard Baudoux. The left-wing mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France told the AFP news agency the attack showed a tolerance by Israel's right-wing government for settler violence.
The mayor said the settlers kicked him and beat him with iron bars, throwing him to the ground.
"It's the gratuitous nature of the violence that stuns me," he said. "They arrived completely enraged."
"The whole world needs to know what's happening there. For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here," he said.

title: Anti-government protesters battle with police in Albania
summary: There were violent clashes between demonstrators and riot police throughout Saturday in the capital Tirana.
body:
Watch: The BBC reports from Tirana, where violent protests grew on Saturday
Demonstrators and riot police fought pitched battles in the centre of Tirana on Saturday for the fifth day in a row.
Masked protesters, many of them high school and university students, hurled rocks and petrol bombs at riot police trying to defend the education ministry, one of the focal points of the protests.
The police responded with water cannon and volleys of tear gas, sending the crowds scattering. There are also reports that rubber bullets were used for the first time.
Protests which began in the summerhave grown into a wider anti-government movement, with calls for the prime minister to resign following corruption allegations linked to his administration.
Many of the protesters in central Tirana wore gas masks or face masks, while volunteers handed out syringes of saline eyewash to reduce the pain from the tear gas which billows down the street.
The constant boom of petrol bombs could be heard exploding on Saturday.
During the afternoon, the focus of the protests shifted to the office of Prime Minister Edi Rama on the city's main boulevard.
Here the crowds swelled to far larger numbers than on previous days.
Riot police faced a steady hail of cobble stones and fireworks, and responded with barrage after barrage of tear gas, some of the canisters landing far back in the crowds, causing panic.
Incensed by the gas, the crowds waited for it to clear, then renewed their attacks.
Demonstrators come equipped to clean tear gas from people's eyes
Black smoke from a burning vehicle and the sirens of police cars and ambulances split the afternoon.
As dusk fell, police special forces arrived to reinforce the riot police.
Many people have been injured on both sides, 80 people have been charged with disorder so far, and hundreds more have been arrested, or are under investigation.
The centre of the Tirana looks increasingly like a war zone, scattered with broken glass and burnt debris.
George, a 19-year-old medical student who works as an electrician to fund his studies, stood near the burnt-out education ministry building, a scarf wrapped round his face and goggles covering his eyes.
He is one of the thousands who have taken part in the increasingly intense protests which began in early June.
In his gloved hands he clutched two rocks intended for the police.
Asked if he was concerned about injuring them, he said: "We have mothers too. We have family too.
"We were peaceful for 135 days. Now we are trying to do like in France… we are trying to make a revolution.
"Our government doesn't want peace, so we are using violence."
Klodi, 21 and Klea, 17, were among the young student protesters in Tirana on Saturday
Many of the protesters were even younger. Klea, 17, is in her first year of university in Tirana.
She said: "All the students are boycotting their university classes and left school to fight for our rights."
She alleged there were provocateurs among the protesters, smashing up stores and banks, to discredit the demonstrations.
Protesters and riot police fought running battles throughout the day in the centre of the capital
Socialist Party Prime Minister Edi Rama has been in power for 13 years and has dominated Albanian politics, much like his main rival Sali Berisha, of the opposition Democratic Party, did for decades.
The students say they are against "the whole corrupt political class". So what is the alternative?
Osman Stafa, a prominent journalist for the News24 channel, who also describes himself as an activist for change, called for a "neutral, caretaker government for one year, to organise new elections".
The irony for the wider European community during this latest wave of unrest is that Rama has long been viewed favourably by the EU, which Albania aspires to join.
In a social media post on Saturday morning, he urged Albanian to "not forget that we have achieved extraordinary things".
He blamed the protests on the opposition Democratic Party, and on what he called "the sinister agenda of foreign actors, intent on halting our progress" towards EU membership, which he has promised by 2030.
He did not name which "foreign actors" he had in mind.
Protesters threw bricks at police on the city's main boulevard
The latest protests have seriously tarnished Rama's carefully cultivated image as a charming leader, steering his country towards prosperity.
Parallel to the protests, a series of investigations by the special prosecution service also threaten his rule.
Set up under EU and US pressure in 2019, the prosecutors recently arrested the powerful secret service chief Vlora Hyseni.
She stands accused of helping a prominent businessman, former government official, and personal friend of Rama, Ergys Agasi, evade justice. The 39-year-old is under arrest.
Agasi, speaking through his lawyer, denied the allegations against him and said he had nothing to do with corruption. Hyseni told prosecutors that she contacted Agasi to try to recruit him to the intelligence services.
Several Albanian media outlets claim he acted as an intermediary between the prime minister and organised criminal groups.
Rama has admitted that he knows Agasi but denies any knowledge of illegal transactions.
"Edi Rama is caught between a rock and a hard place," Lutfi Dervishi, a political analyst and university lecturer, told the BBC.
"He's the victim of his own success. By concentrating so much power in his own hands, he has made himself the only person the people blame for their grievances."
Rama's Socialist Party has a comfortable majority, with 83 out of 140 seats in the Albanian Parliament. The next parliamentary elections are not due till 2029.

title: At least 17 dead in crush at Hindu festival event in India
summary: Many more have been injured at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark a Hindu festival.
body:
At least 17 people have been killed and many more injured in a crush at an event in the Indian city of Kolkata to mark the Hindu festival of Durga Puja, officials say.
The incident occurred during sudden rainfall, which witnesses say prompted a surge of people to try to seek shelter.
West Bengal's Chief Minister Suvendhu Adhikari said a seven-year-old girl was among the dead, and that 25 people were being treated for injuries.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as a "tragic" incident and said the regional government was providing help to affected families.
Six of the dead have been identified, Adhikari said.
A senior police official told the AFP news agency that an announcement caused "commotion" after it started raining and the crowd started "pushing, pulling and rushing forward and fell on the ground, leading to the stampede.".
Deadly crowd incidents, including during religious festivals, are not uncommon in India due to poor management and lack of adequate safety precautions.
Two years ago,121 people were killed in Uttar Pradeshduring a Hindu religious gathering.

title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
summary: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
body:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.
Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.
The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.
The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".
Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.
Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.
What is the Budget and what could be in it?
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.
Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.
Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.
The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.
Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.
Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.
Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects."
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.
He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.
Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".
He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".
Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.
"Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added.
"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.
Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder
Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
A Treasury spokesperson said: "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

title: Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?
summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk showcased the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
body:
A new version of Tesla's Roadster electric sports car, equipped with thrusters which apparently allow it to hover and turn in mid-air, has been unveiled in Texas.
"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," the car firm's CEO Elon Musk said as he presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.
Musk said an audience was needed to prove the car "is not AI", before showing a demonstration of the Roadster driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air, and landing using air jets.
But there are several reasons we're unlikely to see a flying car on our roads anytime soon, as the BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman explains.

title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
summary: After Primark announced plans for home delivery, we hear from women who never go into clothes stores.
body:
Jess says returning online purchases is less hassle than shopping in person
Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online.
As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says.
"The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough.
Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on".
And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection".
Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22.
But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark nowplans to launch a home delivery service in Britain.
Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases.
The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes.
Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein.
Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic.
Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019.
Internet shopping has also been boosted by thedecline of the High Streetin many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town."
Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online.
"I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says.
"I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important."
Julia does most of her shopping online, but likes going into book stores
Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted.
The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces."
Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically.
"I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed."
The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule.
Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale".
However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete.
"Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks.
"When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time."
But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have startedcharging a fee if customers make frequent returns.
This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor".
"Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again."

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
summary: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
body:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
summary: The culture secretary says the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
body:
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division.
Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape.
Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal.
"We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said.
ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries".
The two companies announced in Julythat Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service.
The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here.
It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix.
What Sky buying ITV could mean for your favourite shows
But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up.
In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including:
The need for free expression of opinion in news media
The need for a range of views in news media across the UK
The need for a range of people controlling the media across the UK
The need for a wide range of programmes to be offered across the UK
The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV.
Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added.
But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV.
The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued.
This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added.
Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns.
A Sky spokesperson said: "We havealready made clear commitmentsto protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices."
An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process.
"This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries."
Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration.
This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes.
She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes."

title: Ex-top official Robbins reaches settlement with government over sacking
summary: Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson.
body:
Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as the top official in the Foreign Office in April
Sir Olly Robbins has reached an out-of-court settlement with the government, after he was sacked as the top civil servant in the Foreign Office over the vetting of Lord Mandelson to be US ambassador.
Sir Olly was fired by then Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer earlier this year, after it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.
The FDA union, which represented him in the legal action, said Sir Olly had been made a "scapegoat" to "mask the misjudgement" of Sir Keir.
How much Sir Olly received in the settlement has not been made public.
It came after he requested a judicial review over the decision to dismiss him.
A government spokesperson said Sir Olly "had a distinguished public service career over three decades".
A statement added: "The government has reached a settlement with Sir Oliver following his dismissal. We will not be commenting further on HR matters."
Lord Mandelson was announced as the UK's ambassador to the US in December 2024, before in-depth vetting had been carried out, and formally took up the role in February 2025 after being granted security clearance.
Just seven months later, he was sacked after further information emerged about his previous friendship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Sir Olly was sacked in April, in the wake of a Guardian story that revealed the peer's security clearance had been granted despite vetting officials raising concerns, with the prime minister later saying he was "furious" he had not been informed at the time.
Sir Keir has previously said he sacked Sir Olly after not accepting his explanation for why clearance was granted, telling MPs in April: "I did ask him, and I did not accept his explanation. That is why I sacked him."
Sir Olly has since defended his role in the process, saying that the government's vetting processes must "remain absolutely confidential".
He previously told MPs that he had not seen the documentation from UK Security Vetting, the government's in-house vetting unit, containing their vetting assessment of Lord Mandelson.
He said that instead, he was given an oral briefing, during which he was told the vetting agency considered Mandelson to be a "borderline case", but that the Foreign Office may wish to grant clearance with "appropriate risk management".
Starmer sacks top Foreign Office official after Mandelson vetting revelations
Key evidence from sacked official at heart of Mandelson vetting row
Dave Penman, head of the FDA union, said: "This settlement may bring an end to the Judicial Review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.
"The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgement of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations - which is quite the feat.
"We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process."
Sir Olly said: "I am grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time.
"I want to thank the FDA for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life".
Sir Olly, who was appointed to the Foreign Office job in early 2025, has held a number of senior civil service roles and was previously the government's lead official during Brexit negotiations with the EU.

title: Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
summary: On his first substantive trip to Scotland since becoming PM, he says politicians should focus on solutions "right now" and move beyond the issue of Scottish independence.
body:
The prime minister has invited the Scottish government to work together to put "power back in the hands" of regions - but insisted they must "move beyond" the constitutional question of Scottish independence.
Andy Burnham said he wanted to start work on a new deal for regional economic development in the next few months, including an offer of devolution from the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP).
Speaking at an event in Motherwell, Burnham called on first minister John Swinney to cede further powers from Holyrood to local areas before that happened.
SNP minister Stephen Flynn said the party had asked for increased devolution since theSmith Commission report was publishedin 2014.
The prime minister said devolution "was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament" when Holyrood opened in 1999.
He said it was meant to be the "start of something deeper" where "communities had more of a say in their own future".
Burnham invites Swinney to work together on 'deeper Scottish devolution'
However, he described Scotland as the most devolved nation in the UK but "one of the most centralised in Europe".
"During my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland's regions and cities," he said.
"Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.
"This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people."
Burnham to visit Scotland during SNP conference
Burnham - Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas decisions coming 'shortly'
The Scottish government set out plans for a radical rethink of the country's regional authorities last month.
A new two-tiered system would see the32 local authorities replaced with six new regional authorities.
They would have power over major issues such as economic growth and education.
Below that, between 120 and 160 community authorities would govern more local issues, such as licensing and town centre improvements.
It would be the most significant change to Scotland's regional makeup since the current system was introduced by the UK government in 1996.
Burnham acknowledged that the Scottish government was working on local government reform, but said this had to "move faster".
It is not clear exactly what powers might be exercised at regional level other than employment support.
Burnham appears to expect the Scottish government to devolve some of its own powers to regional authorities.
But he made clear that he will not impose a model of regional devolution like the metropolitan mayors that already operate in England.
Instead he wants to try and agree a way forward with further discussions when the prime minister sits down with all the devolved first ministers at the end of this month.
John Swinney denied that too much power was centralised at Holyrood
Burnham also called for an end to "tribal politics" between the Scottish and UK governments.
He said he and Swinney "agreed on some things" but "didn't have to agree on everything".
Swinney is expected to promote his renewed push for independence in his keynote speech at the SNP conference on Saturday.
He previously welcomed Burnham telling MPs thata border poll would be considered in both Scotland and Northern Irelandif there was a clear consensus and public opinion had changed.
But Burnham later pushed back on that by telling Swinney at a meeting in Glasgow that a second Scottish independence referendum remains "off limits".
Asked whether devolving power more locally in Scotland would make independence more or less likely, the prime minister said: "I don't want to be the last PM of the UK.
"I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions.
"In my view, people in Scotland are suffering from the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else, and I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people right now."
He added: "Too much time is wasted on those dramas, it consumes too much energy."
Stephen Flynn - who was the SNP's leader at Westminster before becoming the Transport Secretary at Holyrood - said the Scottish government would welcome the opportunity to be handed more power over the country's economic prospects.
He said: "Interestingly the first minister sent a letter to the prime minister on Monday where he outlined a number of points he would like to see engagement on.
"This was number seven on that list, so we will of course engage with the prime minister fully in respect of his announcement today."
Before Burnham's speech, First Minister John Swinney said he was interested in "working constructively" with Westminster, adding he was "all for the Scottish Parliament having as many powers" as possible.
UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham should be focusing on creating new opportunities in the energy sector.
She said: "This regional devolution plan is more jobs for the boys. What Andy Burnham should be doing is granting new oil and gas licences in the north sea."
"Devolution is a process, not a solution."

title: Police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
summary: Downing Street says Sarah Helm, the wife of Jonathan Powell, "does not represent the government in any capacity".
body:
Jonathan Powell is the government's national security adviser
Police are assessing a social media post by the wife of the government's national security adviser Jonathan Powell which referenced Palestine Action, a group labelled a terrorist organisation by the Home Office.
Sarah Helm wrote on the social media site X: "God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action."
She was responding to a discussion on Sky News about the author Sally Rooney, whose novels will not be supplied to booksellers in the UK following her announcement that she intends to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A No 10 spokeswoman said Helm was "an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity". The BBC has attempted to contact Helm for comment.
On Friday, a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said: "We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action.
"It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required."
Reform UK MP Danny Kruger has written to the prime minister raising concerns about Helm's post.
The Campaign Against Antisemitism said the post was "gobsmacking".
"Spouses are entitled to independent views, but plainly Mr Powell, who leads on our country's national security and has been intricately involved in our Middle East diplomacy, must publicly denounce this rhetoric if he is to continue in post," the group said.
However, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Sarah Helm is speaking absolute common sense and should be commended for her bravery."
He called for Palestine Action to be de-proscribed "immediately", calling its official labelling as a terror group "ludicrous and authoritarian".
Helm is an author and journalist, who has previously worked at the Sunday Times and as a foreign correspondent for the Independent.
Palestine Action describes itself as a "direct action movement" that uses "disruptive tactics".
Earlier this year, four of the group's activistswere jailedafter causing £1.2m of damage at a UK site of an Israel-based defence firm.
In 2025, the UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group, saying it would not "tolerate" organisations that put the UK's national security at risk.
The proscription made it a criminal offence to belong to or support Palestine Action, punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
The government's decision triggered a wave of protests, which saw an estimated 3,700 people arrested in the UK for publicly expressing their support for the group.
Around 2,500 have been charged, but the cases have not gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription is due to be heard in the Supreme Court next month.
Powell began his government career as a diplomat but later served as an adviser in Tony Blair's government, where he was credited with negotiating a peace deal in Northern Ireland.
In 2024, Sir Keir Starmer appointed him as national security adviser, a position he retained when Andy Burnham became prime minister.

title: Reform councillor quits over offensive remarks
summary: Alan Feeney was captured on undercover filming calling Asian homeowners "parasites".
body:
Alan Feeney has stepped down as deputy mayor of Solihull, and given up his role as a councillor in both Solihull and Birmingham
Warning: This report contains racist and offensive language.
A Reform UK councillor filmed calling Asian homeowners "parasites" has resigned from two councils and apologised for his comments.
Alan Feeney, who has since stepped down from the party, was heard making the remarks duringundercover filming for an ITV News investigation,externalin the run up to council elections in May.
Feeney said he had resigned every post he held on Solihull Council and Birmingham City Council, adding that his remarks "were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable".
He has also been suspended from his job with the prison service, with the Ministry of Justice [MoJ] describing the comments captured during the documentary as "despicable".
In July, his register of interests with Solihull council recorded he was employed as a custodial manager, a position described on the HM Prison and Probation Service website as "the most senior uniformed officers in a prison".
Feeney was one of several Reform members featured in the ITV investigation, which was gathered over the course of a year.
In it, while campaigning in the run-up to May's elections, Feeney described an area as "infested" with Asian families and called them "absolute parasites".
He was also recorded saying no more than 1% of the UK population should be non-white.
Writing on Facebook on Friday, Feeney said he wanted "to offer my sincere and unreserved apologies for the comments I made in the recording that has recently come to light".
He added the comments did "not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report".
These were communities he had "supported countless times" over many years, he added.
He stated his true self was reflected in more than a decade of public service, but achievements "cannot reduce the impact of what has been said".
Feeney, who defected from the Conservative Party to Reform last year, was elected to the Shard End ward on Birmingham City Council in May.
A spokesperson for Reform Solihull said Feeney was briefly with the party, but spent the majority of his time as a Conservative councillor, and did not reflect "the views of the group".
The MoJ has stated the comments featured in the documentary would be investigated and action taken in line with its policy.
Undercover reporters also filmed with two other Reform candidates in Solihull - Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan.
On Friday, Solihull Council's leader of the opposition, Reform's Samantha Gethen, said all three councillors had now resigned, which "was the right thing to do", adding that there would now be by-elections.
Comments reported this week "were offensive, hurtful and wrong", Gethen said.
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Friday, Reform MP Robert Jenrick said he "didn't like what I heard in the documentary" but argued that the party had acted quickly, removing or suspending those in the undercover film.
He added that all parties had "bad apples" and denied it was any more of a problem in Reform than other parties.
On Thursday, the party told the BBC that Feeney had "mutually agreed" to resign from the party.

title: Housing loans granted while Burnham was mayor investigated by councillors
summary: A senior councillor says concerns have been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.
body:
Loans made to property companies - including three controlled by Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owner - while Andy Burnham was Greater Manchester mayor are being investigated by councillors.
About 50 developers have been lent more than £1bn between them from a fund managed by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) since 2015.
John Leech, the chairman of the GMCA's Overview and Scrutiny Committee, told the BBC concerns had been raised about the transparency of the process to approve the loans.
"We just want to be clear that there is a transparent rather than an opaque process," said Leech, who is the Liberal Democrat opposition leader on Manchester City Council.
He said the approval process had been criticised as "very opaque in the past and that it's not necessarily been clearly understood why X was successful and Y wasn't".
A GMCA spokesperson said it was supporting the committee with its enquiries.
Downing Street did not comment.
The money came from the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Loan Fund (GMHILF).
The fund was set up in 2015 with an initial £300m of government investment to help developers build new homes across Greater Manchester.
Three property companies ultimately controlled by Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan were granted loans worth about £55m in total.
The decisions to approve these loans were taken in 2017, in two meetings which were both chaired by Andy Burnham when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.
The decisions to grant loans from the fund were taken publicly by all members of the GMCA, not the mayor alone.
One of Manchester's leading property developers, Renaker, has received the majority of the £1bn lent out from the fund.
Renaker has been involved ina long-running legal battleover £140m worth of loans made to the developer through the GMCA's fund.
A rival developer, Aubrey Weis, claims the the loans were unfair subsidies.
In June, the Court of Appeal found there had been "no error of law" in the GMCA's decision to provide the loans but Weis is appealing the decision.
The Overview & Scrutiny Committee, which reviews the activities of the mayor and the GMCA, agreed to launch an inquiry into the loans earlier this year and Leech is now taking that work forward, after being elected chairman recently.
Leech, a former Lib Dem MP in Manchester, said he felt the fund was intended to be for property companies struggling to access financing.
In 2015, when the loan scheme was launched,Bill Enevoldson, the GMCA's chief investment officer, said,external: "It is not designed to finance unviable projects but can unlock currently unfundable ones."
An evaluation of the fund,externalfrom 2025 said it was designed to provide loans for "projects which might otherwise struggle to secure financing".
Leech said it was "not unreasonable" to ask why seemingly successful businesses needed to borrow public money through this loan scheme.
"In the case of Abu Dhabi, you would imagine that they wouldn't have any problem accessing funds from elsewhere as well," Leech said.
"And so the process clearly does seem to be out of kilter with what the original stated aims were back in 2015."
Leech said the committee had asked GMCA officers to produce a report about the use of these funds.
He said the committee will ask officers questions about the fund at a private meeting, before potentially making recommendations to the Greater Manchester mayor.
The committee does not have the power to sanction the mayor but it can investigate, require answers, expose problems and challenge decisions.
The committee could call forward witnesses, such as current Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig, to give evidence as part of the inquiry.
Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said Burnham had "serious questions to answer" about the loans.
French said "taxpayers deserve transparency over how this money was awarded".
Manchester's relatively strong economic record has been driven in part by a property boom
In a statement, the GMCA said the funding for the loans had been lent "at commercial rates" and had delivered "11,000 new homes and regenerating brownfield land across the city region".
The GMCA said "not a single viable scheme was ever turned down".
A GMCA spokesperson added: "The fund is open to all developers, with lending criteria based on parameters set by the government and developed with external financial experts to reflect due diligence standards in the private sector.
"Every penny loaned from the fund is being fully repaid, delivering billions of pounds worth of development at no cost to the taxpayer."
In 2014, Manchester City Council and Abu Dhabi United Group, which owns Manchester City FC, formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.
Abu Dhabi United Group and Manchester Life were involved in three property developments that were partially financed through the GMCA's loan fund.
A Manchester Life spokesperson said: "It is standard for property development to be funded through a combination of investor equity and borrowing.
"All three sites had previously been derelict. The loans were provided on commercial terms and have been repaid in full, including interest."
The BBC asked Renaker for comment but it did not respond before publication.
Julia Hatmaker, the editor of the Place North West property news website, said viability was "always a struggle" in the development world.
She said the GMCA's loan scheme had been successful in building more homes in the city and generating a return on that investment.
But she said it's a "good time for the combined authority to re-evaluate what kind of project it wants to support with similar loan programmes and whether it wants to put stricter rules in place as to what developments can benefit from them".
